source.title: Diametrical Risk Minimization: theory and computations

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text is the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper trains neural networks with corrupted labels and reports training-fit and test-accuracy outcomes, but its own experiments use 50% label corruption rather than completely random labels or a corruption-fraction sweep.
record.gate_note: The Introduction and Section 5 cite prior work on perfect fitting of noisy or random labels; those cited results are not this paper's results. The paper's own experiments use 50% of training labels flipped to an incorrect class. Figures 2 and 3 report test-accuracy curves and neighborhood-risk distributions; figure-only values are not reconstructed here.
record.test_reason: The standard SGD-ERM controls provide results on memorizing corrupted labels in three-class tasks and on learning useful signal before fitting incorrect labels. These bear on V4's training-fit component and V6. The DRM performance comparisons alone do not test these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that DRM improves generalization and resists overfitting in their corrupted-label experiments, with empirical evidence of flatter solutions. They present these experiments as preliminary support and identify substantial remaining algorithmic and hyperparameter questions.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares parameter-perturbation DRM with standard SGD-ERM, using 50% label corruption and test-accuracy/empirical-risk-landscape outcomes; it does not reproduce the cited random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by method (SGD-ERM versus SGD-DRM), dataset and architecture; DRM test-accuracy degradation differs between the fully connected CIFAR-10 model and ResNet20.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD-DRM preserves test accuracy better than SGD-ERM and generally produces flatter local empirical-risk landscapes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimizing worst-case neighborhood risk can improve generalization under substantial label corruption.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet20 trained with SGD-ERM has lower test accuracy than its DRM counterpart.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DRM improves test accuracy relative to ERM in the tested corrupted-label ResNet20 setting.

record.problems: Own experiments use only 50% corrupted labels, not completely random labels or a corruption-fraction sweep. Test-accuracy values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. Training-fit outcomes are qualitative and the text does not state zero training error for the reported experiments.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters relative to clean-label training.
Random-versus-real-label fitting time and convergence as corruption fraction increases. DRM's reported 3–5-fold overhead compares algorithms instead.

A corruption-fraction sweep, steadily increasing test error toward chance, and perfect training fit throughout that sweep. Only the 50%-corrupted MNIST SGD-ERM training-fit component is explicitly established.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
Separate learning curves for correctly and incorrectly labeled examples, fully random-label comparisons, and direct identification of the shared patterns learned.

missing.what: Explicit nearly zero training-error statement and final SGD-ERM empirical risk at zero, omitted from R2.
missing.locator: Section 5.1, introductory setup and final paragraph discussing Figure 2d

missing.what: The initial generalizing phase before fitting incorrect labels is omitted from the extracted values. Verdicts on V6 use these explicit textual trajectory descriptions.
missing.locator: Section 5.1 discussion of Figures 2a–b; Section 5.2 discussion of Figure 3a

record.verdict_notes: Missing coverage is not evidence against a version. A single corruption fraction cannot establish or refute smooth degradation across fractions. The supplied text includes explicit training-fit and temporal-order evidence that the record overlooked.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites prior work on fitting noisy labels but does not itself test completely random labels, chance test error, or unchanged hyperparameters against a true-label condition.
No comparison of training time for fitting random versus true labels, or sweep over corrupted-label fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Only 50% label corruption is tested; there is no sweep from no corruption to fully random labels. The paper does not report that training error remains perfect across a sweep.
No tests of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The paper cites prior work on noisy-label fitting but does not measure whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.
